highlights: Gas leverage with tighter state control

frictionVectors.title: European gas dependence
frictionVectors.details: Algeria retains strong control over hydrocarbons and uses pipeline and LNG exports to preserve leverage with Europe. Long-term European diversification and volatile prices constrain that influence.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel border pressure
frictionVectors.details: Instability in Mali, Libya, and Niger raises cross-border security and smuggling risks. Algiers is wary of foreign military expansion near its borders and prioritizes strategic autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: External control of hydrocarbons
frictionVectors.details: Angola is pursuing stronger national participation and diversification, but oil revenues, foreign operators, and external finance still dominate fiscal stability. Debt exposure and declining production limit bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Lobito Corridor competition
frictionVectors.details: The United States, European partners, China, and Gulf actors are competing for influence around the corridor linking Angolan infrastructure to critical minerals in the Copperbelt. Luanda gains investment options but faces pressure over ownership and strategic alignment.

frictionVectors.title: Niger trade disruption
frictionVectors.details: Relations with Niger and broader Sahel political authorities have complicated transit, border commerce, and plans tied to regional energy infrastructure. Benin is seeking alternative routes while protecting the strategic role of Cotonou.

frictionVectors.title: Coastal security exposure
frictionVectors.details: Militant spillover from Burkina Faso and Niger threatens northern communities and transport corridors. Expanded foreign security assistance improves capacity but creates dependence on external intelligence and equipment.

frictionVectors.title: Diamond-sector concentration
frictionVectors.details: Botswana retains comparatively strong control over diamond revenues and has pressed international partners for greater local value capture. Demand volatility and dependence on global trading networks remain structural vulnerabilities.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals positioning
frictionVectors.details: Foreign investors are increasingly interested in Botswana's copper, nickel, and other minerals. Gaborone has room to negotiate from a position of institutional strength, though processing capacity remains limited.

frictionVectors.title: Gold-sector nationalization
frictionVectors.details: The government is seeking greater state control over gold production, trading, and strategic mining assets. Weak oversight, insecurity, and opaque partnerships risk replacing one extractive model with another.

frictionVectors.title: Russian security dependence
frictionVectors.details: Reliance on Russian-linked security support has expanded as relations with Western partners deteriorate. This may strengthen regime survival in the short term while increasing diplomatic isolation and uncertainty for foreign investment.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-Mineral Contract Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Burundi is seeking greater state control over gold and rare-earth projects, but limited capital and technical capacity leave it reliant on foreign operators and opaque contract structures.

frictionVectors.title: Regional Security Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Relations with Rwanda remain strained over armed-group accusations and border restrictions, complicating trade corridors and regional infrastructure integration.

frictionVectors.title: External Finance Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Port, airport, energy, and digital infrastructure depend heavily on European, Chinese, and multilateral financing, creating leverage despite strong regulatory institutions.

frictionVectors.title: Tourism and Maritime Vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: The economy remains exposed to external tourism cycles and maritime-security threats, including trafficking routes and disruption around key Atlantic shipping lanes.

frictionVectors.title: Oil, Gas, and Mining Control
frictionVectors.details: Foreign firms and lenders remain central to hydrocarbons, mining, and transport infrastructure, limiting domestic value capture and increasing competition over concession terms.

frictionVectors.title: Anglophone Conflict and Corridor Risk
frictionVectors.details: Insurgency in the Northwest and Southwest continues to threaten roads, plantations, and resource logistics while weakening the state's effective control over peripheral territories.

frictionVectors.title: Security-for-Resources Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Russian-linked security structures retain major influence over regime protection and mining access, reducing transparency and constraining independent state control of strategic resources.

frictionVectors.title: Transport and Border Fragmentation
frictionVectors.details: Poor roads, armed-group checkpoints, and instability along Sudan and Chad routes impede customs revenue and leave critical supply corridors dependent on external security support.

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline and Oil-Finance Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chad's export economy remains tied to the Cameroon pipeline and foreign oil operators, leaving fiscal sovereignty exposed to transit fees, production disputes, and external financing conditions.

frictionVectors.title: Sudan Spillover and Foreign Bases
frictionVectors.details: The Sudan war is driving refugee, arms, and cross-border militia pressures, while the rebalancing of French and other foreign security relationships creates uncertainty around strategic autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Mayotte and maritime jurisdiction
frictionVectors.details: The unresolved dispute with France over Mayotte limits Comoros' effective control of surrounding waters and maritime resources. French administration and security presence remain central to the island's status.

frictionVectors.title: Aid and infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: Transport, energy, and public-service projects rely heavily on external donors and Gulf, French, and multilateral financing, narrowing domestic policy autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Cobalt and copper bargaining power
frictionVectors.details: Chinese firms and other foreign investors remain deeply embedded in the copper-cobalt sector, while Kinshasa seeks stronger contract terms, local processing, and greater fiscal capture.

frictionVectors.title: M23, Rwanda, and mineral corridors
frictionVectors.details: Conflict in the east weakens state control over borderlands and enables illicit flows of gold, tin, tantalum, and tungsten. Regional security competition continues to intersect with access to trade and mineral routes.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon concentration
frictionVectors.details: The economy and fiscal system remain heavily dependent on offshore oil, leaving sovereignty vulnerable to price cycles and the bargaining power of international energy companies.

frictionVectors.title: Debt-linked infrastructure exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese participation in roads, ports, and other infrastructure provides critical connectivity but has increased concerns over debt, project transparency, and strategic dependence.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign participation in energy expansion
frictionVectors.details: New offshore oil and gas development improves fiscal and energy prospects, but international operators retain significant technical and commercial leverage over strategic assets.

frictionVectors.title: Cocoa value-chain sovereignty
frictionVectors.details: Côte d'Ivoire is expanding domestic processing and regulatory control, while EU traceability and deforestation rules could shift bargaining power and impose costly compliance demands on producers.

highlights: Foreign bases crowd the security space

frictionVectors.title: Port and logistics dependence
frictionVectors.details: Djibouti's economy depends on external use of its ports and transport links to Ethiopia, creating leverage for foreign operators and exposure to Ethiopian political and economic shocks.

frictionVectors.title: Competing military presences
frictionVectors.details: U.S., Chinese, French, Japanese, and other foreign military facilities generate revenue and protection but constrain independent security policymaking amid Red Sea and Gulf rivalries.

frictionVectors.title: External Financing Dependence
frictionVectors.details: IMF programs, Gulf investment, and asset sales provide vital liquidity but constrain Cairo's policy autonomy over strategic infrastructure and state-owned enterprises.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea and Canal Security
frictionVectors.details: Attacks and instability around the Red Sea continue to threaten Suez Canal revenues, shipping security, and Egypt's regional economic leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Controlled Energy Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Declining oil output and dependence on external technical and financing partners limit the state's ability to convert offshore resources into broad-based sovereign wealth.

frictionVectors.title: Opaque Resource Governance
frictionVectors.details: Weak transparency and concentrated political control increase exposure to foreign commercial leverage while reducing domestic oversight of energy revenues and infrastructure deals.

frictionVectors.title: Regional Port Competition
frictionVectors.details: Eritrea's coastline and ports remain strategically valuable, but rivalry involving Ethiopia, Gulf states, and Red Sea powers creates pressure over access and security arrangements.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-operated mining remains a central source of hard currency, leaving sovereign revenue and infrastructure priorities vulnerable to commodity cycles and external partners.

frictionVectors.title: Dependence on South African Corridors
frictionVectors.details: Trade, fuel supply, electricity, and logistics remain heavily tied to South Africa, limiting Eswatini's room to independently manage strategic infrastructure and external shocks.

frictionVectors.title: Fiscal and Industrial Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Customs revenues and foreign investment underpin state finances, while limited industrial diversification leaves the kingdom exposed to external market and donor leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Nile Basin Tensions
frictionVectors.details: The Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam strengthens Ethiopia's control over its electricity and water strategy but continues to generate acute friction with Egypt and Sudan.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Finance and Telecom Access
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring, Chinese infrastructure exposure, and the opening of telecom and financial sectors bring capital and technology while creating new leverage for external actors.

highlights: Manganese and oil remain strategic anchors

frictionVectors.title: Foreign mining leverage
frictionVectors.details: The transition authorities are seeking greater state participation and local processing in manganese and iron projects, creating friction with established foreign operators and investors.

frictionVectors.title: Port and rail dependence
frictionVectors.details: Export corridors and logistics remain dependent on external capital and expertise, limiting Libreville's ability to fully control the value chain.

highlights: Fisheries and trade corridors are strategic

frictionVectors.title: Foreign fishing access
frictionVectors.details: Licensing arrangements and limited monitoring capacity expose Gambian fisheries to foreign overexploitation, weakening food and resource sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Senegambia infrastructure reliance
frictionVectors.details: The country's trade and energy security remain closely tied to Senegalese transport links and external development finance.

highlights: Gold remains the core sovereignty asset

frictionVectors.title: Illicit gold mining
frictionVectors.details: Illegal mining damages land and water while diverting gold revenues, often through opaque domestic and foreign trading networks.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-mineral competition
frictionVectors.details: Foreign interest in bauxite, lithium, and other minerals is increasing, but fiscal constraints and infrastructure needs give outside investors significant negotiating leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Simandou foreign control
frictionVectors.details: The iron-ore corridor is dominated by large Chinese-linked and international consortia, leaving Guinea dependent on external finance, technology, and export infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Transition legitimacy crisis
frictionVectors.details: The junta's prolonged rule and restrictions on political activity create domestic instability that could threaten contracts, infrastructure, and investor confidence.

frictionVectors.title: Cashew value-chain dependence
frictionVectors.details: Guinea-Bissau exports most cashews with minimal local processing, leaving farmers and state revenues vulnerable to foreign buyers and price swings.

frictionVectors.title: Illicit maritime networks
frictionVectors.details: Weak institutions and limited maritime surveillance create openings for narcotics trafficking and opaque fishing activity, undermining control of territorial waters.

highlights: Port and energy sovereignty under pressure

frictionVectors.title: External debt and infrastructure finance
frictionVectors.details: IMF-linked reforms and large repayment obligations constrain Nairobi's policy autonomy. Chinese, Gulf, and Western partners compete for influence over transport, energy, and digital infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Mombasa and critical minerals
frictionVectors.details: Mombasa remains strategically important to foreign shipping and security interests, while emerging critical-mineral projects raise concerns over local value addition and licensing transparency.

frictionVectors.title: Lesotho Highlands Water Project
frictionVectors.details: Water transfers to South Africa provide essential revenue but deepen dependence on Pretoria and expose Lesotho to disputes over pricing, construction delays, and project governance.

frictionVectors.title: Textile and infrastructure vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: The textile sector remains exposed to external trade preferences and shifting supply chains. Limited fiscal capacity leaves major infrastructure and energy projects reliant on foreign donors and investors.

frictionVectors.title: Iron ore and mining concessions
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-led iron ore and gold operations provide badly needed revenue but continue to raise concerns about tax capture, environmental damage, labor conditions, and limited domestic processing.

frictionVectors.title: Port and logistics competition
frictionVectors.details: Monrovia and Buchanan ports attract competing commercial and geopolitical interest. Liberia's need for investment can weaken its negotiating position on long-term concessions and infrastructure control.

frictionVectors.title: Competing control of oil infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Rival political and armed networks can disrupt production, export terminals, and budget flows. Foreign states and private actors seek leverage through security partnerships and energy contracts.

frictionVectors.title: Mercenaries and migration routes
frictionVectors.details: External military and security involvement continues to complicate reunification of national institutions. Control of southern routes and coastal facilities links Libya's sovereignty to wider Mediterranean and Sahel bargaining.

frictionVectors.title: Nickel, cobalt, and mineral dependence
frictionVectors.details: Large foreign-backed mining projects dominate strategic mineral production and expose Madagascar to commodity-price shocks. Revenue-sharing, environmental impacts, and local procurement remain persistent sovereignty concerns.

frictionVectors.title: Ports, energy, and external finance
frictionVectors.details: Foreign lenders and investors are increasingly important to ports, power, and telecommunications. Weak grid capacity and fiscal constraints reduce the state's ability to enforce long-term national-content objectives.

frictionVectors.title: External Financing Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring, IMF conditions, and foreign-exchange shortages constrain policy autonomy and make fuel, fertilizer, and infrastructure access dependent on external partners.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Concessions and Local Value
frictionVectors.details: Renewed interest in uranium, rare earths, and other minerals could diversify exports, but weak bargaining capacity and limited processing infrastructure risk low domestic capture of value.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Sovereignty Versus Operational Capacity
frictionVectors.details: Bamako is pressing foreign mining firms for larger state participation and revenue, while legal uncertainty, sanctions exposure, and insecurity complicate production and investment.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel Corridor Fragmentation
frictionVectors.details: The withdrawal from regional security arrangements and reliance on Russian-linked security support have reduced Western leverage but increased risks to transport, energy, and mineral corridors.

highlights: Gas Exporter at a Strategic Crossroads
Iron Ore and Green Hydrogen Ambition

frictionVectors.title: Offshore Gas Governance
frictionVectors.details: The Greater Tortue Ahmeyim project with Senegal offers major export potential, but revenue sharing, border coordination, local content, and delivery delays remain politically sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Controlled Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese, European, Gulf, and other investors are central to mining, ports, renewable power, and hydrogen plans, creating financing opportunities alongside exposure to external bargaining pressure.

frictionVectors.title: Chagos Settlement Implementation
frictionVectors.details: The sovereignty dispute over the Chagos Archipelago remains tied to the future of the Diego Garcia military facility, making the issue a continuing test of Mauritius's strategic autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Blue Economy and Financial Scrutiny
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius seeks greater control over maritime resources and ocean infrastructure while balancing dependence on foreign capital with international pressure on financial transparency.

highlights: Phosphate Power Meets Green Industrial Policy

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara Resource Diplomacy
frictionVectors.details: Phosphate, fisheries, ports, and renewable projects linked to Western Sahara generate investment and leverage for Rabat but continue to trigger legal and diplomatic challenges.

frictionVectors.title: Water and Energy Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Desalination, renewables, and interconnection projects strengthen resilience, yet drought, imported fuels, and dependence on foreign technology and capital remain structural vulnerabilities.

highlights: LNG Restart Hangs on Cabo Delgado Security

frictionVectors.title: Cabo Delgado Insurgency
frictionVectors.details: Insurgent violence continues to threaten communities, transport corridors, and the timetable for TotalEnergies-led LNG development. Foreign security assistance improves protection around strategic sites but limits independent state control.

frictionVectors.title: LNG and Debt Dependence
frictionVectors.details: International energy companies and lenders retain substantial leverage over Mozambique's future gas revenues. Fiscal stress increases pressure to prioritize external financing and investor confidence over local value capture.

highlights: Oil and Green Hydrogen Race Accelerates
State Seeks Stronger Local Value Capture

frictionVectors.title: Offshore Oil Ownership
frictionVectors.details: Recent offshore discoveries have attracted major international operators, creating opportunities for revenue growth while raising concerns over contract terms, environmental risk, and domestic participation.

frictionVectors.title: Critical Minerals Competition
frictionVectors.details: Uranium, lithium, and green-hydrogen projects draw investment from European, Chinese, and Gulf-linked actors. Namibia is attempting to retain more processing, jobs, and infrastructure benefits through tighter policy coordination.

frictionVectors.title: Uranium and Mining Reorientation
frictionVectors.details: The military authorities are renegotiating the country's relationship with French-linked mining interests while seeking alternative partners. This increases perceived sovereignty but risks technical, financial, and export disruptions.

frictionVectors.title: Sanctions and Corridor Pressure
frictionVectors.details: The withdrawal from regional security and political arrangements complicates access to coastal trade corridors and external finance. Niger is deepening ties with Sahel partners and Russia, but replacement infrastructure and logistics remain limited.

highlights: Oil Reform Meets Production and Security Constraints

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Capital in Oil and Gas
frictionVectors.details: The government is using licensing reform and new investment incentives to revive production, while international majors and trading firms retain major influence over technology, finance, and export channels.

frictionVectors.title: Power and Transport Bottlenecks
frictionVectors.details: Grid instability, fuel-market disruption, and insecure transport corridors constrain industrial growth and domestic resource processing. Chinese, Gulf, and Western infrastructure financing expands capacity but can deepen contractual and debt dependence.

highlights: Regional Security Leverage Draws External Pressure

frictionVectors.title: Critical Minerals Transit
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda remains a major trading and processing hub for minerals from the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, generating foreign-exchange and logistics advantages. Allegations of support for M23-linked networks expose Kigali to sanctions, diplomatic pressure, and reputational risk.

frictionVectors.title: External Aid and Security Partnerships
frictionVectors.details: Western aid, Gulf investment, and security cooperation support Rwanda's state capacity and infrastructure ambitions. These relationships also give outside actors leverage over regional military policy and governance conditions.

frictionVectors.title: Gulf of Guinea exploration
frictionVectors.details: Unproven offshore petroleum prospects attract foreign operators, but limited state capacity leaves São Tomé and Príncipe dependent on external capital and technical expertise.

frictionVectors.title: Fisheries and maritime enforcement
frictionVectors.details: Illegal fishing and weak patrol capacity undermine control over valuable waters, increasing reliance on outside maritime-security partners.

frictionVectors.title: Oil and gas contract renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The government is seeking greater domestic value capture and transparency from offshore projects, creating tension with international operators and lenders.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: Heavy financing needs make Dakar reliant on multilateral creditors and foreign contractors, limiting room for rapid economic-policy shifts.

frictionVectors.title: Tuna access and foreign fleets
frictionVectors.details: Seychelles benefits from fisheries revenues but must balance licensing income against concerns over foreign-fleet dominance and sustainable stock management.

frictionVectors.title: External security infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Cooperation with India and other partners supports maritime surveillance, while the government carefully manages sovereignty sensitivities around foreign security facilities.

frictionVectors.title: Iron ore and mineral concessions
frictionVectors.details: Large-scale mining remains vital to exports and public revenue, but foreign ownership, concession terms, and local processing continue to limit domestic value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor dependence
frictionVectors.details: Freetown’s logistics and power systems require substantial foreign financing and contractors, exposing strategic infrastructure to external commercial leverage.

highlights: Ports and security shaped by outsiders

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of ports and maritime assets
frictionVectors.details: External security partners and commercial operators play decisive roles in port development, maritime protection, and access to prospective offshore resources.

frictionVectors.title: Federal-regional sovereignty disputes
frictionVectors.details: Disagreements between Mogadishu, federal member states, and Somaliland complicate licensing, revenue sharing, and the enforcement of national resource claims.

highlights: Ports and power remain strategic bottlenecks

frictionVectors.title: Grid and port dependence
frictionVectors.details: Electricity reliability and congestion at Durban and other ports constrain industrial sovereignty. Private capital and foreign-linked operators are increasingly important to restoring infrastructure capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Mineral beneficiation pressure
frictionVectors.details: South Africa is seeking greater local processing of platinum-group metals, manganese and rare-earth inputs, while competing investors push for secure export access and favorable regulatory terms.

highlights: Oil revenue remains the state lifeline

frictionVectors.title: Oil-transit dependence
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan relies on infrastructure and transit arrangements through Sudan to monetize its oil, leaving revenue and production vulnerable to Sudan's conflict and pipeline disruptions.

frictionVectors.title: External security and investment leverage
frictionVectors.details: Regional governments, international donors and foreign energy firms retain substantial influence over security, fiscal management and petroleum operations amid weak domestic institutions.

highlights: War fragments control of strategic assets
Gold and ports attract competing patrons

frictionVectors.title: Gold-war economy
frictionVectors.details: Gold production and smuggling networks help finance rival armed actors, while foreign buyers and regional intermediaries compete for access to Sudanese mineral flows.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea infrastructure contest
frictionVectors.details: Port Sudan and associated transport corridors are strategic lifelines exposed to military contestation and external bargaining by Gulf, regional and other foreign powers.

highlights: Ports and LNG drive strategic competition

frictionVectors.title: LNG and fiscal-control negotiations
frictionVectors.details: Tanzania is pressing for stronger domestic benefits from offshore gas development, balancing investor certainty against demands for local content, revenue retention and environmental safeguards.

frictionVectors.title: Corridor and port competition
frictionVectors.details: Dar es Salaam and emerging regional corridors face competition from neighboring ports, with Chinese, Gulf and Western interests seeking influence over logistics and mineral-export infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor dependency
frictionVectors.details: Lomé's importance as a Gulf of Guinea transshipment and hinterland corridor gives foreign shipping, finance and logistics actors significant leverage over national infrastructure priorities.

frictionVectors.title: Phosphate-sector control
frictionVectors.details: The state retains a central role in phosphate development but faces pressure to attract external capital while improving domestic processing, transparency and value capture.

frictionVectors.title: EU Migration Bargaining
frictionVectors.details: European financing and migration cooperation give Brussels influence over Tunisian policy. Domestic resistance limits how far the government can align publicly with external demands.

frictionVectors.title: Energy Import Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Tunisia remains vulnerable to imported energy, fiscal stress, and delayed investment in domestic renewables. This constrains strategic autonomy despite strong state control over key infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: EACOP Financing and Sanctions
frictionVectors.details: The East African Crude Oil Pipeline is advancing with Chinese and regional backing but faces Western political pressure, financing constraints, and environmental opposition. Uganda retains ownership ambitions while relying heavily on external capital and logistics.

frictionVectors.title: Lake Victoria and Regional Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Transport, power, and oil links increasingly tie Uganda to Kenya, Tanzania, China, and Gulf investors. These connections improve market access but create exposure to competing regional and external interests.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Mining Dominance
frictionVectors.details: Copper and cobalt remain central to Zambia's fiscal future, but foreign operators retain major control over capital, technology, and export channels. Lusaka is seeking stronger tax, local-processing, and state-participation terms without deterring investment.

frictionVectors.title: Lobito Corridor Competition
frictionVectors.details: The Lobito Corridor offers an alternative to routes through Tanzania and South Africa while attracting US, European, and Gulf interest. New infrastructure could diversify Zambia's options but may also deepen external competition over mineral access.

frictionVectors.title: Lithium Processing Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Zimbabwe is using export restrictions and beneficiation demands to retain more value from lithium, but Chinese and other foreign firms still dominate investment, processing capacity, and market access. Limited domestic finance and technology weaken bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Gold and Diamond Leakage
frictionVectors.details: Gold smuggling, opaque mining networks, and sanctions-related financial restrictions reduce state revenue and complicate formal trade. The government is tightening oversight while remaining dependent on politically connected intermediaries and external buyers.
